## What is data

- Data are a collection of information that can be used to make inferences, draw conclusions and make decision <br><br>
    - **Structure Data**: has a *well-defined* organization which simplifies analysis<br><br>
    - **Unstructured Data**: does not have a well-defined organizational strategy, requires extra effort to analyze<br><br> 
- Literature Reviews, Experiments (simulations), Surveys, Field-work can all be thought of as different methods of data generation

::: {.notes}

## Why analyze data

- **Implicit Assumption: ** *Within the data, there exists knowledge*<br><br>

- By *formally analyzing* data using recognized and validated approaches, we might
    - discover/understand the potential knowledge that is encoded in our data
    - add credibility/justification to our arguments (i.e., our potential discovery/understanding)
    - add some *objectivity* to discovery

::: {.notes}


:::

## Different types of data

- **Quantitative data:** Measurements, numeric/scaled survey results, counts,...
    - Statistics is a branch of mathematics interested in developing methods for quantitative data analysis<br><br>

- **Qualitative data**: Transcripts, field-notes, journals/books, open-ended survey results,...
    - In qualitative data analysis, *(en)coding* is the act of creating quantitative data representations based on qualitative data
    - Resulting coded data can be analyzed with traditional statistical tools

## Different types of quantitative data

- **Data matrix:** a standard format for recording and organizing the properties (i.e., factors and response variables) of objects (i.e., experimental units) in a study<br><br>

- **Nominal data:** data that can be categorized in discrete categories when order of category has no meaning<br><br>

- **Ordinal data:** data that can be categorized in discrete categories when order of category means something<br><br>

- **Continuous data:** data that can take on any value within a range<br><br>

:::

## A typical data analysis work flow

- **Clean/Structure**: organize your data into a data matrix; identify errors, missing data, etc. <br><br>

- **Visualize**: determine a strategy to view/show your data <br><br>
  
- **Describe**: extract/calculate some summary statistics and "metrics" that help explain the overall data <br><br>

- **Decide**: use the data to make an inference (for example, conduct a hypothesis test), make a prediction (for example, build a model and extrapolate behaviour)<br>


## An introduction to Microsoft Excel

- MS Excel is a spreadsheet management software tool 
    - Spreadsheets existed well before modern computers. They were literally large sheets of paper divided into rows and columns made of “cells”
    - Modern software spreadsheets are powerful because cells can be updated dynamically through formulas using cell references; allows users to make fairly complex models to see how one input can change several outputs<br><br>
- MS Excel has several built-in functions that make data analysis convenient, including tools for visualization, description and decision-making

::: {.notes}

- show students how to copy the outputs from a filter to another column and compute an average, standard deviation
- show students how to create a new processed value (size_score=body*width^2+weight)
- show students how to use averageif function
- tell them will look at some t-tests and the like during lecture module 6
:::

## An introduction to R/Rstudio

- R is a programming language
    - First appeared in 1993
    - The language grows continuously as developers create new or improve existing functions (and other reusable packets of code) over time
    - The language has several functions that make data analysis convenient, including
    functions for visualization, description and decision-making
    - Currently at R version 4.6.1 (released June 2026)<br><br>
    
- RStudio is a software tool that makes editing and working with R code easier

::: {.notes}
- Open up the entomology data set
- show student how to look at column names, create data filters (use filters of species) 
- show students how to copy the outputs from a filter to another column and compute an average, standard deviation
- show students how to create a new processed value (size_score=body*width^2+weight)
- show students how to use averageif function
- tell them will look at some t-tests and the like during lecture module 6
:::

## Thoughts on Code vs Spreadsheets

- You can accomplish simple (and sophisticated analysis) using codes and spreadsheets
- Code becomes preferable as data sets becomes larger (spreadsheets use A LOT of memory)
- Code is preferable for *portability* (i.e., it's easy to share code with other people) and *re-analysis* (i.e., you can re-use the same code with new data really easily)
- Code is preferable when doing complex statistical analysis
